message.content:
Painting the Eiffel Tower isn’t a quick weekend job – it’s a multi‑year undertaking.  
A rough back‑of‑the‑envelope calculation goes something like this:

| Item | Estimate |
|------|----------|
| Total exposed metal surface | ≈ 18 000 m² |
| Typical coverage rate per painter (including prep, priming, topcoat, drying time) | ≈ 10 m² per day (≈ 1 m² per hour) |
| Number of painters that can actually work simultaneously (due to access, safety, scaffolding limits) | 5–10 people |

If you had a full‑time crew of 10 painters working 8‑hour days, the raw “paint‑on‑the‑surface” time would be:

\[
\frac{18\,000 \text{ m²}}{(10 \text{ m²/day} \times 10 \text{ painter})} \approx 180 \text{ days}
\]

That’s **180 person‑days** of actual paint application. In practice, however, you can’t keep 10 painters on the tower all the time because of:

* **Access constraints** – only a handful of workers can safely climb and work on the structure at once.
* **Safety & logistics** – setting up scaffolding, ensuring fall protection, coordinating traffic, etc., add significant overhead.
* **Drying & curing** – each coat needs to dry before the next layer can be applied; weather delays are common.
* **Multiple coats** – a typical restoration involves a primer, several intermediate coats, and a final protective coat.

All of that pushes the schedule out dramatically. Historically, major restoration projects on the Eiffel Tower have taken **2–3 years** from start to finish when a dedicated crew works continuously under optimal conditions. If you’re looking at a smaller crew or intermittent work (e.g., doing one section at a time), the timeline could stretch to **4–5 years** or more.

So, while the math suggests a few hundred person‑days of pure painting, the real-world constraints mean you’re looking at a **multi‑year effort**—typically **2–3 years** for a full, high‑quality restoration.
